assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, trapping neutral atoms at the magic wavelength so that Doppler, recoil and lattice light shifts cancel, opened a route to fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 and beyond. This is a conceptual invention (Katori's magic-wavelength proposal) plus its realization, and it has changed what can be measured: tests of relativity and gravitational redshift at the millimetre scale, searches for varying constants and dark matter, and a path to redefining the second.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice idea and demonstrated early Sr clocks; Jun Ye's group drove the record-setting accuracy, quantum-degenerate and many-body clock work and comparison technology. The two-person configuration is clean, though Pierre Lemonde, Hidetoshi Katori's and others' contributions and the neighbouring ion-clock and comb work (already recognised in 2005 and 2012) leave some boundary questions.
assessment.maturity: Independently reproduced in many national laboratories and in commercial-grade devices; performance has improved by orders of magnitude over about two decades and clock networks are operating. Timing is mature and the field is well past the proof-of-principle stage.
uncertainties: Exact share of credit relative to other lattice-clock groups that I cannot verify from the longlist alone.
Whether the committee views this as sufficiently distinct from the earlier frequency-metrology prizes.
The redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so the ultimate practical consequence is still pending.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cold atoms in optical lattices realised the Hubbard model with tunable parameters, giving direct observation of the superfluid to Mott insulator transition, fermionic Hubbard physics and quantum gas microscopy. It created a new, clean way to study strongly correlated matter, and the Hubbard-model proposal by Jaksch and Zoller supplied the theoretical foundation.
assessment.attribution: Zoller provided the central theory (with Jaksch) for realising the Bose-Hubbard model; Greiner, Bloch and Esslinger delivered the key experiments. Greiner's role in the 2002 Mott transition and the gas microscope is decisive, but the prize can accommodate only three, and I select Bloch, Zoller and Esslinger as theory plus experiments across bosons and fermions. Reasonable alternatives exist and the allocation is genuinely contested.
assessment.maturity: The field is well-established with many groups and benchmarking against condensed-matter theory and numerics, now over twenty years old. Recognition is timely; the Bose-Einstein condensation prize of 2001 was a prerequisite.
uncertainties: Four credited names compete for three slots; Greiner's omission is arguable.
Overlap with the quantum computing and simulation candidate that also features Zoller.
Quantitative advantage over classical simulation for open problems is still being established.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect from spin-orbit coupling in graphene and its observation in HgTe quantum wells launched the field of topological insulators, linking band topology with edge transport. It has broad lasting impact across condensed matter, though my own judgement of this area is from the outside of atomic physics.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the decisive theoretical prediction and the Z2 classification; Molenkamp led the experimental confirmation in HgTe wells based on the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal. The BHZ theorists and the 3D topological insulator work (Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Hasan) are not in this credit set, so the configuration omits some contributors but is workable.
assessment.maturity: Experimentally confirmed in HgTe and later in 3D materials; interpretation is stable and the topic is widely taught. Application impact is still developing, but the physical concept is mature.
uncertainties: The omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang from this entry creates a credit gap I cannot resolve.
Overlap with the other topological insulator entry that includes Qi-Kun Xue and quantum anomalous Hall.
The 2016 prize already recognised topological phases, so novelty relative to that award is a question.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit quantum electrodynamics applies cavity QED ideas to superconducting artificial atoms in microwave resonators, providing strong coupling, dispersive readout and the architecture used for superconducting quantum processors. It is a clear instance of transferring quantum optics concepts to a new platform with real consequences for quantum technology.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin and Schoelkopf wrote the 2004 proposal and the 2004 experiment, so Wallraff is a missing contributor in this credit set; among the supplied names Schoelkopf (experiment, transmon and readout), Girvin (theory) and Blais (theory) are consistent with the discovery. The 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits touched adjacent territory, which shapes how a second award would be viewed.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced and developed worldwide, and a base for commercial quantum computers; interpretation is stable. Timely, though the 2025 award may reduce appetite so soon after.
uncertainties: Absence of Andreas Wallraff and Alexander Wallraff-related experimental co-credit from the supplied names.
Recent 2025 award in a nearby area may affect timing.
Whether the prize should recognise the architecture or the later device engineering.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Electromagnetically induced transparency and its use for slow light, stopped light and light storage show coherent control of the optical response of a medium. These effects underlie atomic and solid-state quantum memories and have lasting importance for quantum optics. I have professional familiarity with slow light and storage in rare-earth crystals, and I flag that this is my own research neighbourhood so I weigh it conservatively.
assessment.attribution: Harris established EIT theory and early demonstration, including slow light in hot gases; Hau demonstrated 17 m/s light in a Bose-Einstein condensate and light stopping. Imamoglu contributed to early theory (lasing without inversion, EIT proposals) and Fleischhauer, Lukin and Phillips-Walsworth storage work are additional claimants; I propose the two with the most decisive experimental and conceptual roles.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced many times in atoms and solids and used in memories and sensing; the physics is stable. Recognition is somewhat late rather than premature.
uncertainties: Conflict of interest: my own work on slow light and optical storage in crystals is closely related, which could bias me.
Credit among Harris, Hau, Imamoglu, Fleischhauer, Lukin and others is not fully separable.
Practical consequences for quantum networks are still developing.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum cascade laser, an intersubband semiconductor laser designed by band-structure engineering, gave compact room-temperature mid-infrared sources and enabled trace-gas sensing and spectroscopy. It is an original invention with clear lasting use in measurement.
assessment.attribution: Faist, Capasso, Sivco, Sirtori, Hutchinson and Cho produced the 1994 device; Cho's molecular beam epitaxy growth was essential, and Kazarinov and Suris proposed the idea in 1971. A two- or three-person split is difficult, and I choose Capasso and Faist on conceptual leadership, noting that this is contestable.
assessment.maturity: Technologically mature since the 1990s with commercial adoption; the science is stable. Recognition is overdue rather than premature, though the question is whether the contribution is a physics discovery or an engineering invention.
uncertainties: Kazarinov and Suris priority is outside the credited names.
Cho and the Bell Labs co-inventors compete for credit.
Fit with the physics prize rather than an engineering recognition is uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene predicted flat bands from moire interference and was shown to host correlated insulators and superconductivity, creating the field of twistronics and moire quantum matter. It is original, highly influential and has spawned a large literature.
assessment.attribution: The Bistritzer-MacDonald theory predicted the magic angle and Jarillo-Herrero's group delivered the decisive 2018 experiments with Cao and colleagues; the credit set captures theory plus experiment. Junior experimental co-authors such as Yuan Cao are not eligible from this list.
assessment.maturity: Replicated widely, but the nature of the superconductivity and correlated states is still debated and the discovery dates from 2018, so recognition may be somewhat premature.
uncertainties: Mechanism of superconductivity remains unresolved.
Students and postdocs who made the first measurements are outside the credit set.
Prize timing is early compared with typical committee practice.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cavity optomechanics established radiation-pressure coupling of light and mechanical motion, with sideband cooling to the quantum ground state, optomechanical squeezing and entanglement, and sensitive force and displacement readout. It is conceptually close to LIGO-style measurement and to my interest in measurement limits.
assessment.attribution: Aspelmeyer, Kippenberg and Vahala each made major contributions: Vahala and Kippenberg with microcavity radiation-pressure and cooling, and Aspelmeyer with quantum-regime experiments and reviews. Braginsky's earlier theory and others such as Painter and Teufel are outside this set, so allocation is contested.
assessment.maturity: The quantum regime has been reproduced in several platforms, but applications are still developing and the field is partly an elaboration of earlier ideas, so recognition may be slightly early.
uncertainties: Credit overlap with Painter, Teufel, Harris, Marquardt and Braginsky.
Impact beyond a research field is still limited.
Whether it is separate enough from the recognised LIGO and cooling work.
